title: Mobile credentials and internal API disclosure
summary: What did the service trust once it recognized the application making a request? I separated the application's identity from the member's identity. The two checks protected different information.

findings.name: Credentials distributed in a mobile release
findings.evidence: I found credentials packaged in the released application. My highest-priority report covered the risk of distributing a reusable application identity to everyone who installs the client.

findings.name: Internal API information disclosure
findings.evidence: I compared the responses for a missing, invalid and recognized client identity. A separate client identifier found in published documentation opened an internal specification covering 44 endpoints and exposed additional reference metadata. Member-only operations still required an authorized session.

method: On a separate autocomplete lead, I borrowed a question from e-commerce ranking research. What can a ranked suggestion reveal before anyone opens the underlying record? I compared the information surfaced by discovery with what was already public. That helped me separate bulk visibility of profile metadata from access to private member records.
decision: I prepared five reports from 13 leads. I held eight back, including a data set that was public by design and a service description whose operations still required a client certificate. I recommended enforcing permissions per operation and reviewing which credentials a public build can carry.

papers.title: Seasonality Based Reranking of E-commerce Autocomplete Using Natural Language Queries

title: Browser trust, OAuth registration and account isolation
summary: A browser policy, a sign-in prompt and an ownership check can all sit between a visitor and the same record. I evaluated each separately so I could tell an engineering team which boundary had actually failed.

findings.name: Cross-origin trust on seven hosts
findings.evidence: Seven hosts reflected an untrusted web origin and advertised support for credentials. I captured that behavior on sign-in redirects. A redirect established the policy error. Reading a signed-in user's private response remained an unverified impact.

findings.name: Open OAuth client registration
findings.evidence: The service accepted my test application without administrator review. Six follow-up authorization attempts still required fresh sign-in and MFA. The rating depended on whether unreviewed registration violated the intended trust policy. The numerical score and its vector disagreed in my notes, so I retained the provisional qualitative rating.

findings.name: Sign-in method disclosure
findings.evidence: The sign-in service returned authentication-method metadata before login. A nonexistent address also received a response, so a successful lookup alone could not establish that a particular person had an account.

method: In one research pass, I mapped 20 research and advisory references to 17 candidate test scenarios. For ownership, I used a taxonomy of broken object-level authorization to group the failure modes, then borrowed the multi-identity comparison from AuthProbe to choose my controls. My account could receive its own event stream. Other streams stayed restricted, and ownership checks held across 18 API paths. Those controls kept a real browser-policy error from becoming an unsupported claim about access to other accounts.
decision: I recommended an explicit allowlist of trusted browser origins and a review of who can register applications. During the review I lowered eight preliminary severity ratings as the controls narrowed what I could show.

papers.title: Broken Object Level Authorization in the Wild
AuthProbe: Specification-Driven, Multi-Identity Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Recruitment API

title: Identity-verification data in ordinary profile responses
assessment: Critical if real · Low if seeded
summary: A newly provisioned account associated with a demo workspace could read identity-verification fields for 49 of 50 sampled profiles. The sensitivity was clear. The unresolved question was whose data the workspace contained.

findings.rating: Critical if real · Low if seeded
findings.name: Identity-verification fields visible to the demo account
findings.evidence: The detailed profile response included legal-name, age, country and verification-date fields. In a separate comparison, one profile view included email addresses that a sibling view omitted for the same caller. The records did not establish whether the values belonged to real people or which relationships the caller was intended to have.

findings.name: Working account provisioned without an invitation
findings.evidence: I obtained a working account without supplying an invitation. The product also offered invite-based onboarding. The security impact depended on whether open signup was intentional and which records the resulting demo-associated account was meant to see.

method: I kept the caller fixed and varied the view of the same kind of profile. Comparing individual fields revealed a privacy decision that a pass/fail check on the whole response would have missed. I then counted how often the sensitive fields were present across the sample.
decision: I recommended verifying the origin of the records first, then applying a shared field allowlist based on the caller's role and relationship to the profile. A retest with fictional identities in separately owned workspaces would settle the outstanding access question.

title: Session approval, exposed feedback and sign-in telemetry
summary: I verified an account-takeover scenario end to end with my own account. The flaw was in the handoff between the person approving sign-in and the session that received the credentials.

findings.name: Approval granted a different session access to my account
findings.evidence: After I approved sign-in on my test account, a separate session under my control received usable access and refresh credentials. User interaction was required. I could demonstrate the consequence entirely within accounts and sessions I controlled.

findings.name: Private feedback readable without sign-in
findings.evidence: I read 100 production feedback records without signing in to a user account. They included account identifiers, device details and feedback text. The 100 records are the observed sample size.

findings.name: Sign-in codes disclosed to analytics providers
findings.evidence: I traced sign-in codes into three third-party analytics integrations. That established disclosure to the providers. Use of the codes by a third party was outside the evidence.

method: For the session flaw, I tracked who approved the action and who received the resulting capability. I applied a similar distinction to messaging: establishing a connection, receiving routing information and reading message content are separate outcomes. My method notes cite research on what push-notification services can see. I did not observe another user's message or notification.
decision: I recommended binding each approval to the initiating session, limiting feedback reads to the roles that need them, and excluding sign-in secrets from analytics events.

papers.title: The Medium is the Message: How Secure Messaging Apps Leak Sensitive Data to Push Notification Services

title: Tenant isolation and service-account password hashes
summary: The application enforced resource ownership in my staging tests. The database role assigned to the tenant could read password hashes belonging to internal service accounts.

findings.name: Internal service-account password verifiers exposed
findings.evidence: From the tenant context I could read stored password verifiers for internal accounts. That exposure creates an offline password-guessing risk. I did not recover a password, assume an internal role or demonstrate a tenant escape.

findings.name: Internal infrastructure information visible to a tenant
findings.evidence: The tenant role could also read operational settings that described the service's internal infrastructure. Separately, permission checks indicated write access on internal operational tables. I left those tables untouched.

findings.name: Inconsistent anti-automation controls at sign-in
findings.evidence: In staging, an alternative sign-in flow issued a session for my own valid credentials without the challenge shown in the browser. Production evidence established only that the flow was recognized.

method: I inspected the same tenant identity at two layers. At the application layer, an inaccessible resource and a nonexistent one returned the same result. At the storage layer, I reviewed the privileges the tenant role actually inherited. That exposed an internal boundary the application's ownership checks did not cover.
decision: I recommended narrowing inherited tenant privileges and reviewing the exposed service credentials. The staging review used one tenant account. A cross-tenant conclusion would require a separate, independently controlled tenant.
